title: Store the Record
content:
What problem does this solve?
Programs become useful when information has names. A variable lets you store a value, use it later, and replace it when the situation changes.

Start with the behavior
  count = 4
  print(count)
The first line stores 4 under the name count. The second line asks for the value currently stored there.

Values can change
  count = 2
  count = count + 3
After the second assignment, count stores 5. Python evaluates the right side first, then stores the result on the left.

Numbers and text are different values
  days = 3
  status = "OVERDUE"
Quotes make OVERDUE text. Without quotes, Python would look for a variable with that name.

Vocabulary after the behavior
The = in these examples is assignment. Using a variable's current value to calculate a new value is an expression. Assigning a new value to an existing name is reassignment.
concepts: Assignment stores a value under a name
Using a variable reads its current value
The right side of an assignment is evaluated before the result is stored
Quoted text and numbers are different kinds of values

examples.title: Store and read
examples.explanation: count stores 4, then print reads that stored value.

examples.title: Change a value
examples.explanation: Python calculates 2 + 3 first, then stores 5 back in count.

examples.title: Expedition record
examples.explanation: Names make the changing facts reusable.

common_mistakes: Reading = as 'is equal to' instead of 'store this value in this name'
Copying a literal into print() instead of using the variable the exercise asks you to practice

exercises.title: Read a variable
hints: count stores the number 4 before print(count) runs.

exercises.title: Store a number
exercises.prompt: Change the assigned number so the program prints exactly 7.
hints: The printed value comes from steps.
Change what is stored in steps; do not change print(steps).

exercises.title: Store text
exercises.prompt:
Create a variable named status containing the text ready, then print the variable. The output should be exactly:
ready
hints: status needs to store text, not a bare name.
Put ready inside quotes when you assign it.

exercises.title: Follow reassignment
hints: Read the lines from top to bottom.
On the second line, the old value of count is 2, so the right side becomes 2 + 3.
Python stores 5 back in count, so print(count) shows 5.

exercises.title: Literal text needs quotes
exercises.prompt: Repair the program so status stores text and the output is exactly OVERDUE.
hints: Python is looking for a variable named OVERDUE.
The intended value is literal text.
Put quotes around OVERDUE in the assignment.

exercises.title: Expedition record
exercises.prompt:
Create these variables exactly:
expedition = 17
registered = 4
days_overdue = 3
status = "OVERDUE"

Then print the four values in that order by using the variable names. Do not copy the literal values into the print() calls.
exercises.starter_code: # Store the four facts, then print the variables
exercises.reference_solution:
expedition = 17
registered = 4
days_overdue = 3
status = "OVERDUE"

print(expedition)
print(registered)
print(days_overdue)
print(status)
hints: Create the four assignments first so every fact has a name.
After the assignments, print expedition, registered, days_overdue, and status—not 17, 4, 3, and "OVERDUE" directly.
Use four assignments followed by print(expedition), print(registered), print(days_overdue), and print(status).

tests.message: Print the stored variables rather than copying the literal values.

exercises.success_message: The record now stores its facts separately from how they are displayed.
